body:
Origin and development

Kathakali is a classical dance-drama of Kerala that acquired its distinctive form mainly during the 17th century. Its name combines words meaning story and play.

Its development drew upon earlier Kerala performance traditions, particularly Krishnanattam, Ramanattam and regional theatrical conventions. Ramanattam, associated with Kottarakkara Thampuran, presented narratives based on the Ramayana.

Kathakali combines dance, dramatic representation, poetry, vocal music, percussion, costume and elaborate makeup. Unlike dance forms primarily presented as solo recitals, it is especially associated with the dramatic representation of stories through multiple characters.

Literature and repertoire

Kathakali narratives commonly draw upon the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas. Its dramatic compositions are known as Attakkatha, literary texts written for performance through dance and drama.

In a traditional Kathakali performance, singers present the narrative while the actors communicate its meaning through gestures, facial expressions and movement. The literary language frequently combines Malayalam and Sanskrit elements.

Traditional performances were predominantly presented by male actors, who also portrayed female characters. Women now participate in Kathakali as well.

Character types and makeup

One of the most distinctive features of Kathakali is its system of identifying the nature of a character through facial makeup, costume and headgear. These categories are examples of Aharya Abhinaya, or expression through external appearance.

Makeup categoryTypical character association
Pacha (green)Noble and heroic characters
Kathi (knife)Proud, arrogant or villainous characters
Thadi (beard)Different powerful character types represented by distinctive beards
Kari (black)Characters such as demonesses and certain fierce figures
Minukku (shine)Gentle or refined characters, including sages and many female roles

Thadi itself includes different beard-colour categories with different character associations. For example, a red beard commonly indicates a fierce or aggressive character, whereas a white beard is associated with characters such as Hanuman.

The large layered skirts, elaborate crowns, ornaments and conspicuous painted faces make Kathakali visually distinctive. Chutti is the characteristic raised white border used around the lower face in several makeup categories.

Music and instruments

Kathakali music is rooted in Kerala's regional musical tradition and draws upon Sopana and Carnatic influences. Vocalists and percussionists are essential to the presentation.

  • Chenda: A cylindrical percussion instrument producing a powerful sound.
  • Maddalam: A double-headed drum.
  • Chengila: A metallic gong.
  • Elathalam: A pair of metallic cymbals.

The Hasta Lakshana Deepika is an important textual authority associated with hand gestures in Kerala performance traditions, including Kathakali.

Preservation and major exponents

The Malayalam poet Vallathol Narayana Menon, together with Manakkulam Mukunda Raja, established Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930. Located at Cheruthuruthy in Thrissur district, the institution played a major role in preserving Kathakali and other classical performing arts of Kerala.

Prominent Kathakali exponents include Guru Kunchu Kurup, Kalamandalam Krishnan Nair and Kalamandalam Gopi.

Prelims focus

  • Kathakali is a classical dance-drama of Kerala.
  • Ramanattam and Krishnanattam are important historical antecedents.
  • Attakkatha refers to literary compositions for Kathakali.
  • Pacha represents noble characters; Kathi represents arrogant or villainous characters.
  • Chenda and Maddalam are characteristic percussion instruments.
  • Kerala Kalamandalam was founded in 1930.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Theatre Crafts, pp. 113–118; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 12–13; Kerala Tourism, Kathakali, October 2021, and What is Special about Kathakali Costumes?; Kerala Kalamandalam, institutional history; CBSE, Class 12, Dance: A Survey, Kathakali section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Kathakali: Kerala's Classical Dance-Drama

body:
Origin and meaning

Mohiniyattam, also spelled Mohiniattam, is a classical dance form of Kerala. Its name refers to the dance of Mohini, the enchanting female manifestation of Vishnu in Hindu mythology.

The dance developed within Kerala's temple and court traditions. Its identity is particularly associated with Lasya, the graceful and delicate dimension of Indian classical dance.

Although Mohiniyattam has traditionally been performed as a female solo dance, contemporary presentations also include group performances and other creative formats.

Royal patronage and revival

Swati Tirunal, the 19th-century ruler of Travancore, was an important patron of music and dance. His court contributed to the development and enrichment of Mohiniyattam compositions.

During the 20th century, Vallathol Narayana Menon and Kerala Kalamandalam played important roles in the revival and institutional preservation of the dance. Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma contributed significantly to its teaching, documentation and development.

Repertoire and musical traditions

Mohiniyattam combines graceful rhythmic movement with expressive interpretation. Love, devotion and compassion are recurring themes in its repertoire, although its subject matter is not restricted to them.

Common recital items include:

  • Cholkkettu: An introductory composition based on rhythmic syllables.
  • Jatiswaram: A predominantly rhythmic dance composition.
  • Varnam: A major composition combining rhythm and expression.
  • Padam: An expressive interpretation of poetic or musical content.
  • Tillana: A lively composition emphasizing rhythm.

The musical accompaniment draws upon Carnatic music and Kerala's Sopana musical traditions. Instruments may include the mridangam, edakka, veena, violin, flute and cymbals. Vocal accompaniment communicates the poetic content of expressive compositions.

Characteristic costume

Mohiniyattam is especially recognizable by its off-white or cream-coloured costume with golden borders, traditional gold-coloured ornaments and jasmine flowers. A characteristic hairstyle involves a bun positioned to one side of the head.

Major exponents

  • Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma
  • Kanak Rele
  • Bharati Shivaji
  • Kalamandalam Kshemavathy

Distinction between the 2 Kerala classical dances

FeatureMohiniyattamKathakali
Traditional presentationPredominantly female solo danceCharacter-based dance-drama
Visual identityCream and gold costumeElaborate facial makeup and headgear
Artistic emphasisLasya and graceful expressionDramatic representation of narratives
Characteristic repertoireCholkkettu and PadamAttakkatha-based dramatic compositions

Kerala Kalamandalam contributed to the preservation of both forms. Their common geographical origin and institutional association do not mean that their costumes, performance structures or repertoires are identical.

Prelims focus

  • Mohiniyattam originates in Kerala.
  • Its name is associated with Mohini, a manifestation of Vishnu.
  • Swati Tirunal of Travancore was an important patron.
  • Lasya, cream-and-gold costume and a side-positioned hair bun are characteristic.
  • Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma and Kanak Rele are prominent exponents.
  • Trap: Elaborate Pacha and Kathi character makeup belongs to Kathakali, not Mohiniyattam.

[References: Kerala Tourism, Mohiniyattam — The Classical Dance of Kerala, sections on history, costume and repertoire; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Cultural Packages, Mohiniyattam Dance; Kerala Kalamandalam, institutional material on Mohiniyattam; UPSC Education, Classical Dances of India — Eight Forms, Mohiniyattam section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Mohiniyattam: Kerala's Graceful Classical Dance

body:
Geographical origin

Kuchipudi is named after the village of Kuchipudi in Krishna district of Andhra Pradesh. It developed within the Telugu-speaking region as a tradition combining dance, music and dramatic storytelling.

The form was historically maintained by hereditary male performers, particularly Brahmin performers associated with the Bhagavatulu tradition. These performers travelled and presented religious narratives through dance-drama.

Siddhendra Yogi and Bhama Kalapam

Siddhendra Yogi is traditionally credited with an important role in shaping Kuchipudi and its devotional dance-drama tradition. Accounts differ concerning his precise historical dates, so his contribution is more securely identified through the tradition associated with him.

Bhama Kalapam, attributed to Siddhendra Yogi, is one of the best-known works in the Kuchipudi repertoire. Its central character is Satyabhama, a consort of Krishna. The composition explores her emotions, pride, love and relationship with Krishna through dramatic and expressive performance.

Earlier Kuchipudi performances were predominantly presented as dance-dramas by male performers, who also took female roles. During the 20th century, the solo recital became increasingly important, and women became prominent performers.

Repertoire

Kuchipudi retains both dramatic and purely rhythmic elements. Its repertoire may include invocations, Jatiswaram, Shabdam, Kalapam and expressive compositions.

A distinctive item is the Tarangam, associated with compositions from Narayana Tirtha's Krishna Lila Tarangini. In a characteristic presentation, the performer dances on the rim of a brass plate while maintaining rhythmic movement.

Some presentations also include balancing a vessel, but this is not a compulsory feature of every Tarangam or every Kuchipudi performance.

Music and costume

Kuchipudi uses Carnatic music, with common accompanying instruments such as the mridangam, violin and flute. Telugu literary and musical compositions occupy an important place in the tradition.

Traditional Kuchipudi dance-dramas may include spoken dialogue and introductory passages through which characters identify themselves. This dramatic element helps distinguish the historical Kuchipudi tradition from a purely solo dance recital.

The female solo costume often resembles the Bharatanatyam costume, with a pleated garment, ornaments, ankle bells and decorated hair. Consequently, costume alone is not always sufficient to distinguish the 2 forms.

Major exponents

ExponentAssociation
Siddhendra YogiTraditional shaping of Kuchipudi dance-drama and Bhama Kalapam
Vempati Chinna SatyamDevelopment and popularization of modern Kuchipudi
Raja and Radha ReddyProminent Kuchipudi performers and teachers
Shobha NaiduRenowned Kuchipudi exponent
Vedantam Satyanarayana SarmaTraditional Kuchipudi dance-drama, including female character portrayals

Vempati Chinna Satyam established the Kuchipudi Art Academy in Chennai in 1963. This illustrates how a dance originating in one state can develop influential training centres elsewhere.

Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam compared

FeatureKuchipudiBharatanatyam
OriginAndhra PradeshTamil Nadu
Traditional identityDance-drama and later solo repertoireTemple and court solo tradition
Distinctive associationBhama Kalapam and TarangamMargam and Tanjore Quartet
MusicCarnaticCarnatic

Prelims focus

  • Kuchipudi is named after a village in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh.
  • Siddhendra Yogi is associated with Bhama Kalapam.
  • Satyabhama is the central character of Bhama Kalapam.
  • Tarangam is associated with Narayana Tirtha's Krishna Lila Tarangini.
  • Raja and Radha Reddy and Vempati Chinna Satyam are major exponents.
  • Trap: Carnatic music is common to Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam and cannot distinguish them by itself.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, p. 12; CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 10–11; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Cultural Packages, Kuchipudi Dance; UPSC Education, Classical Dances of India — Eight Forms, Kuchipudi section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Origin in Odisha

Odissi, formerly also spelled Orissi, is a classical dance form originating in Odisha. Its development reflects the interaction of temple worship, devotional literature, regional music and traditional performing communities.

Ancient dance sculptures at Udayagiri and Khandagiri near Bhubaneswar and medieval temple carvings illustrate the historical importance of dance in Odisha. The sculptures of the Sun Temple at Konark also provide important artistic inspiration.

Mahari and Gotipua traditions

Two historical performance traditions are particularly important for understanding the development of Odissi.

  • Mahari: Female temple dancers associated with devotional service, particularly the Jagannath Temple at Puri.
  • Gotipua: Young male performers traditionally trained to dance in feminine costume, presenting devotional compositions and other dance items.

Both traditions contributed to the preservation of regional dance vocabulary and repertoire. Several influential teachers of modern Odissi received training within the Gotipua tradition.

Jayadeva and Gita Govinda

The 12th-century Sanskrit lyrical composition Gita Govinda by Jayadeva occupies an important place in Odissi.

The work describes the relationship between Radha and Krishna, expressing themes of love, separation, longing and reunion within a devotional framework. Its lyrical compositions provide rich material for expressive dance.

The songs commonly known as Ashtapadis from Gita Govinda are frequently interpreted through Odissi Abhinaya.

Distinctive postures

Odissi is especially recognizable through 2 characteristic postures.

  • Tribhanga: A posture involving bends or deflections at 3 principal points of the body: the neck, torso and knees. It produces the characteristic curved appearance associated with Odissi and Indian sculpture.
  • Chauka: A balanced, square-like posture associated with stability and strength.

The Tribhanga posture is not exclusive to Odissi. It also appears extensively in Indian sculpture and other artistic traditions, although it is a particularly important identifying feature of Odissi.

Traditional repertoire

A conventional Odissi recital commonly includes the following compositions:

  1. Mangalacharan: An auspicious opening and invocation.
  2. Batu: A pure dance composition associated with sculptural postures and rhythmic movement.
  3. Pallavi: The gradual rhythmic and melodic elaboration of a dance composition.
  4. Abhinaya: Expressive interpretation of poetry and song, including compositions from Gita Govinda.
  5. Moksha: A concluding composition expressing the idea of spiritual liberation.

Contemporary recitals may vary this traditional sequence.

Music and costume

Odissi is accompanied by the regional Odissi musical tradition. A characteristic percussion instrument is the Mardala, a barrel-shaped drum. Flute, cymbals and vocal accompaniment are also commonly used.

The costume generally consists of a draped or tailored Odisha silk garment accompanied by elaborate silver jewellery. A decorative white headpiece, often resembling the form of a temple tower, is another recognizable feature.

Modern development and major exponents

During the 20th century, several gurus and performers helped reconstruct, organize and popularize the modern Odissi repertoire by drawing upon the Mahari and Gotipua traditions, regional texts, music and sculptural evidence.

  • Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra
  • Guru Pankaj Charan Das
  • Guru Deba Prasad Das
  • Guru Mayadhar Raut
  • Sanjukta Panigrahi
  • Sonal Mansingh
  • Madhavi Mudgal

Sonal Mansingh is associated with both Odissi and Bharatanatyam, illustrating that prominent dancers may specialize in more than one classical form.

Prelims focus

  • Mahari and Gotipua are historical traditions associated with Odissi.
  • Jagannath Temple at Puri and Konark Sun Temple are important cultural associations.
  • Gita Govinda was composed by Jayadeva in the 12th century.
  • Tribhanga and Chauka are characteristic postures.
  • Mardala is a characteristic percussion instrument.
  • Kelucharan Mohapatra is a major Odissi guru.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10, Social Science, 2017 edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, dance section; CBSE, Class 12, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Dance: A Survey, pp. 12–14; Odisha Tourism, Iconic Odisha, Odissi Dance section; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Cultural Packages and Audio-Visual Catalogue, Odissi Dance; UPSC Education, Classical Dances of India — Eight Forms, Odissi section. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]
